current_activity: The 70th Infantry Division settles on Walcheren island, which Hitler ordered held as a fortress
notes: Event date: Schramm, OKW war diary, p. 393, entry of 18 September: "Die 70. Inf.=Div. richtete sich auf der Insel Walcheren ein"; CMH Siegfried Line Campaign ch. 9 p. 218-219: Zangen was Zangen "was to install another infantry division" (the 70th) "on Walcheren Island", and "the divisions operated through no corps headquarters". Event definition: the settling in on 18 September (Schramm); CMH says most arrangements were initiated or completed by 17 September. Event support: the OKW war diary and CMH (two families) agree. Location: Walcheren island with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: an island point. Location support: both sources name the island. Commander: Generalleutnant Wilhelm Daser.

current_activity: General Daser surrenders the 70th Division garrison at Middelburg, ending organised resistance on Walcheren
notes: Event date: CMH Siegfried Line Campaign ch. 9 p. 229: "On 6 November the town of Middelburg fell and General Daser surrendered"; p. 219: "Generalleutnant Wilhelm Daser's 70th Infantry Division"; Lexikon der Wehrmacht, 70. Infanterie-Division, table 1944: November, 15. Armee, Heeresgruppe B, Walcheren. Event definition: the surrender on 6 November. Event support: two source families: CMH for the day and place; the Lexikon table for the army and the island (month-level). Location: Middelburg with a precision of 3 km, the town named for the surrender. Location approximate: a town point. Location support: CMH names Middelburg. Commander: Generalleutnant Wilhelm Daser. Opponents: Canadian First Army, British 1st Commando Brigade and 52nd Division. Context: CMH ch. 9 p. 228-229 puts the garrison at about 10,000 men; the Lexikon table lists the division at Walcheren for November without a day. Review (British Batch 2, 28 October 2026; inferred value; old value: operation_id OP-SCHELDT; new value: operation_id OP-INFATUATE): the row describes the fighting on Walcheren on 2 to 6 November 1944, the assault that Stacey, pp. 379-380 and 407, names Operation Infatuate (Infatuate I at Flushing, Infatuate II at Westkapelle; Ellis, vol. II, p. 114, dates the attack to 1 November and p. 123 the end to 8 November); the new operation is a child of OP-SCHELDT, so the narrower operation replaces the broader one. The Canadian Army row of 8 November (C1283) stays under OP-SCHELDT because it also closes the whole Scheldt battle.
